Answers for every workbook page, the mistakes students make most, and a line to say when they get stuck. A ledger line is also spelled leger line (AMEB accepts both). Some books teach the ledger notes as four lists: A C E above the treble staff, C A F below it, C E G above the bass staff, E C A below it; this book counts out of each land and reads from the five Cs instead. The lists' third notes between the lands (F three ladders under Queensland, G three ladders over Kingsland) come later. AMEB: Preliminary needs one ladder below Queensland; Grade 1 one ladder above and below both lands; Grade 2 up to three.

Left for later: the natural sign and "a sign lasts until the bar line" (the Accidentals room), writing and drilling E♯ = F, B♯ = C, F♭ = E and C♭ = B (the scales chapters, the book says once that a sharp or a flat is not always a black key: E♯ is F), double sharps and flats (Grade 4).

"Counting the key they stand on as the first step (“C, C♯, D: three!”). Skipping the black key and landing on the next white key. From E and B a half step up is a white key: there is no black key on their right."

"Calling every pair of white neighbours a tone. Missing the B C that crosses from one octave into the next. The pattern from C (W W H W W W H) is the major scale's; AMEB and the scales chapter write it T T S T T T S (tone, semitone): accept either."
